title: Compressed Air
summary: Air hoses can whip, tools can disconnect, and compressed air can throw debris. OSHA's rules for pneumatic tools cover securing tools, safety clips, muzzle devices and using air for cleaning.
talking_points: Secure a pneumatic tool to the hose or whip by a positive means so it cannot accidentally disconnect (29 CFR 1926.302(b)(1)).
Install and maintain safety clips or retainers on pneumatic impact tools so attachments cannot be shot out (1926.302(b)(2)).

Pneumatically driven nailers, staplers and similar equipment with automatic fastener feed that operate at more than 100 psi at the tool need a safety device on the muzzle to keep the tool from ejecting fasteners unless the muzzle is in contact with the work surface (1926.302(b)(3)).
Do not use compressed air for cleaning unless it is reduced to less than 30 psi, and then only with effective chip guarding and PPE (1926.302(b)(4)).
Hoses exceeding 1/2-inch inside diameter need a safety device at the source of supply or branch line to reduce pressure in case of hose failure (1926.302(b)(7)).
Never use an electric cord or an air hose to hoist or lower a tool (1926.302(a)(2), (b)(6)).
Good practice: never point an air hose or air-powered tool at yourself or another person.
site_hazards_to_check: Tool attached to the hose with no positive lock
Missing safety clips or retainers on impact tools
Nailer or stapler running above 100 psi with no muzzle safety device
Air used for cleaning at full line pressure
Hose over 1/2-inch inside diameter with no pressure-reducing device at the supply
discussion_questions: How do we keep a pneumatic tool from disconnecting from its hose?
What do we use to clean dust off a surface instead of full-pressure air?
Who checks the hoses and fittings before we start work?
